Introduction Earnings management has received increased attention in recent years from various stakeholders, including legislators, investors, practitioners, and academics. This rising interest arises from the importance of earnings in boosting investor trust and achieving business goals (Eugster and Wagner, 2020). Earnings are an important part of financial reporting since they show the trustworthiness and correctness of financial accounts (Eugster and Wagner, 2020). Moreover, they provide perception into management incentives and motivations, company willingness to take risks, disclosing how these factors affect financial reporting practices and future profits of the firms (Mamatzakis, 2024). Managers and executives may exaggerate earnings to enrich their bargaining power and support organizational goals, affecting shareholders' perceptions and decisions. Corporate governance plays a critical role in curbing earnings management practices within firms. Firms' earnings management varies depending on S the specific methods used to measure earnings managemeSnt and the level of scrutiny and oversight involved. The agency theory emphasizes that coErporate boards protect shareholders' R interests through effective monitoring (Fama and Jensen, 1983). However, the board's ability P to fulfil these responsibilities significantly depends on knowledge, prior experience, and N expertise. Strong corporate governance with an efficient board of directors enhances oversight I of financial practices, which can prevent managers and executives from engaging in aggressive E earning management activities (Zhang et al., 2024). The board of directors, with their diverse L professional backgrounds, past experiences, and personal traits, can have different effects on C firm outcomes, as they bring dIifferent unique skill sets and perspectives that can enhance or T impair the decision-making and outcomes of firms (Bawuah, 2024). Recent studies highlight R that connections through the board of directors are standard in extracting short-term and long- A term firm outcomes (Tiwari et al., 2024). The literature also emphasizes the role of military ties in risk taking (Benmelech and Frydman, 2015) while not addressing how military ties might govern financial reporting. Theoretical Foundation, Literature review and hypothesis development 2.1 Theoretical Foundations This study is anchored in two primary theoretical frameworks: Agency Theory (Meckling and Jensen, 1976) and Upper Echelons Theory (Hambrick & Mason, 1984). These theories provide a conceptual foundation for understanding how military-connected directors influence earnings management and how audit quality moderates this relationship. Agency theory posits that conflicts of interest arise between principals (shareholders) and agents (managers) due to S information asymmetry and divergent goals. Managers may engage in earnings management S to maximize personal benefits, such as bonuses or job security, at the expense of shareholders. E Effective corporate governance mechanisms, includinRg board oversight and external audits, mitigate these conflicts by aligning incentives and Penhancing transparency (Fama and Jensen, 1983). Military-affiliated directors, with their disciplined and ethical training, are likely to act N as strong internal monitors, reducing opportIunistic earnings manipulation. This aligns with the theory’s emphasis on governance struEctures that curb agency costs. Upper Echelons Theory suggests that executives’ backgrounLds, experiences, and values shape their strategic decisions C and organizational outcomes. Military service instills traits like discipline, risk aversion, and I adherence to rules (BenmeTlech and Frydman, 2015), which may translate into conservative R financial reporting. This study extends the theory by demonstrating how military backgrounds A uniquely influence financial reporting integrity, particularly in emerging markets where formal governance mechanisms are weaker. 2.2 Literature review and hypothesis development The integrity and reliability of financial reporting have been of much interest to researchers, with numerous studies examining various aspects that may affect earnings management. The current body of literature identifies the internal and external factors affecting earnings quality. For example, earnings management in non-financial industries is associated with social trust (Sánchez-Ballesta and Yagüe, 2022) market concentration (El Diri et al., 2020), investor rights (Chen et al., 2020) and media coverage (Sánchez-Ballesta and Yagüe, 2022). Environmental conditions also play a significant role and force companies to manage earnings accordingly (Ding et al., 2021). In countries with relatively weak legal systems and high media attention, social trust is negatively associated with earnings management, especially in Chinese non- financial firms (Cao et al., 2022). On the other hand, firms with substantial investor rights, deep 4 ARTICLE IN PRESS institutional ownership and active financial analysts provide less opportunity for earnings management. In the context of macro factors affecting earning quality, (Yung and Root, 2019) used data from 18 countries (2001-2014) to show that firms are more likely to manage earnings when there is policy uncertainty. Zhang et al. (Chen et al.) discovered that external financing dependency has a positive relationship with earnings management. The internal factors affect the earnings quality to a great extent. These internal factors include corporate governance, leadership characteristics, and firm policies, key determinants of earnings quality. The relationship between audit quality and earnings management is multifaceted, particularly within the broader context of corporate governance. High audit quality is generally associated with a reduction in earnings management practices, as it enhances the accuracy of financial reporting and improves the detection of fraudulent activities. However, the effectiveness of audit quality is not universal. it is shaped by various contextual factors, including regulatory frameworks and the strength of corporate governance mechanisms (Baig et al., 2024). Some studies suggest that executives with military backgrounds enhance audit quality by reducing earnings management, while others indicate that such executives may increase earnings manipulation under certain conditions (Lai et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024) Firms led by ex- S military executives often exhibit lower levels of accruSal-based earnings management, suggesting a positive influence on audit quality (Li et al.,E 2024). However, military managers R may engage in real earnings management, which is perceived as less risky, thereby P complicating the relationship with audit quality (Li et al., 2024). These findings underscore the N need for a nuanced understanding of the factors that influence audit quality and earnings I management, particularly in diverse organizational and institutional settings. E Numerous valid arguments support the assertion that the Big Four are well-equipped to L consistently uphold high audit Cquality standards worldwide. Moreover, the Big Four firms I adopt consistent team training, expertise, and identical audit procedures. This uniformity T decreases the probabilityR of endorsing misreporting and offers more substantial incentives for addressing legal conAcerns (Van Tendeloo and Vanstraelen, 2008). The relationship between military connections and earnings management (H1) is rooted in the ethical and disciplined behavior instilled in military-trained directors, which reduces financial misreporting. However, the effectiveness of internal governance mechanisms (such as military-connected boards) can be further reinforced by external monitoring mechanisms, particularly audit quality. Agency theory suggest that high-quality audits mitigate agency conflicts by enhancing transparency and reducing information asymmetry between managers and stakeholders (Jensen & Meckling, 1976). Military-connected directors may already discourage earnings manipulation, but external auditors provide an additional layer of scrutiny, ensuring compliance with accounting standards. Firms audited by Big Four auditors signal credibility to investors (He et al., 2022). Military connections may enhance governance, but audit quality acts as a verifiable signal that financial statements are reliable, further deterring earnings management. The interaction between military connections and audit quality can be understood through two mechanisms: Military directors bring internal discipline, while Big Four auditors enforce external 7 ARTICLE IN PRESS accountability. Prior research shows that Big Four auditors significantly reduce accrual-based and real earnings management (Tantawy and Moussa, 2023). In emerging markets, where institutional oversight is weak, high-quality audits play an even more critical role (Fan & Wong, 2005). Studies find that firms with military-linked directors exhibit lower financial misconduct (Koch-Bayram & Wernicke, 2018). However, the effectiveness of military governance may depend on external checks. (Guedhami et al., 2014) shows that audit quality enhances the credibility of financial reports, and (Fan and Wong, 2005) found that Big Four auditors play a similar role in emerging markets. JSON: Name: military_boards_audit_earnings Title: A panel system-GMM analysis of how military-experienced directors and external audit quality affect accrual-based and real earnings management in Pakistani non-financial firms Short Hypothesis: Firms with military-experienced directors exhibit lower accrual-based and real earnings management than firms without such directors, and this reduction is larger for firms audited by Big Four auditors. Related Work: Prior research evaluates board connections, political ties, and director backgrounds as governance mechanisms and separately evaluates external audit quality as a constraint on earnings management. Existing approaches either: (a) focus on accrual-based or real earnings management in isolation; (b) use cross-sectional or OLS panel regressions with limited controls for endogeneity; (c) treat director connections generically (political or business networks) rather than isolating military experience; or (d) evaluate audit choice or quality without testing interaction effects with specific director backgrounds. Limitations include mixed cross-country findings driven by institutional heterogeneity, few studies combining accrual and real EM measures, measurement gaps for director military affiliation, potential reverse causality and selection into military-linked boards, and sparse attention to the joint (interaction) effect of internal (director) and external (audit) governance. Abstract: This study examines whether the presence of military-experienced directors on corporate boards reduces earnings management and whether external audit quality amplifies that effect. Using a panel of non-financial firms listed on the Pakistan Stock Exchange from 2010–2022, the analysis measures accrual-based manipulation via discretionary accruals and real activity manipulation via abnormal cash flow, production costs, and discretionary expenses. Military affiliation is captured both as a binary indicator and as the ratio of military directors; audit quality is proxied by Big Four engagement. The empirical strategy addresses selection and endogeneity using a two-stage selection framework and a system generalized method-of-moments estimator. The main contributions are (1) introducing military service as a distinct board characteristic affecting earnings quality, (2) jointly testing accrual and real EM outcomes, and (3) quantifying the moderating role of high-quality external audits. Expected results show military-affiliated boards constrain both forms of earnings management and that Big Four audits strengthen this governance effect. Experiments: Dataset: non-financial firms listed on Pakistan Stock Exchange, years 2010–2022; sample: active firms with complete annual reports and ORBIS financials; exclusions: financial sector firms and firms with missing governance data. Variables: dependent — DACC = absolute discretionary accruals (Jones-style residuals); RM measures = RM_1 and RM_2 constructed from abnormal CFO, abnormal production costs, abnormal discretionary expenses (Roychowdhury framework) and combined indices; key independent — MCON (binary if any ex/current military director), RMD (ratio of military directors); moderator — AUQ (binary: Big Four =1); controls — firm size (ln assets), leverage, firm age, industry dummy, capital intensity. Baselines: (A) pooled OLS with year and industry fixed effects; (B) firm fixed effects OLS; (C) IV-probit selection first-stage with inverse Mills ratio second-stage; (D) system-GMM dynamic panel estimator (Arellano-Bover/Blundell-Bond) as primary estimator. Specifications: estimate DACC, RM_1, RM_2 as separate dependent variables; include interaction term MCON*AUQ. Evaluation metrics: coefficient estimates, robust t-statistics, p-values, economic effect sizes (marginal effects), Hansen J-test p-value, AR(1)/AR(2) test p-values, sensitivity of coefficients to clustered robust SEs. Ablations and comparisons: (1) drop interaction term (MCON*AUQ); (2) replace MCON with RMD; (3) separate accrual vs real EM channels and regress each abnormal component individually; (4) subsample tests: state-owned vs private, large vs small firms; (5) placebo test using pre-period pseudo-treatment; (6) alternative audit quality proxies (audit-fee percentile, industry-specialist auditor). Reported outputs: coefficient tables, marginal-effects table for interaction, robustness table across specifications, diagnostic test statistics (Hansen, AR), and pre-registered analysis script. Risk Factors and Limitations: Measurement error in military affiliation (titles/roles may be ambiguous) and audit-quality proxies (Big Four binary coarse); residual endogeneity and selection bias despite system-GMM and selection correction (unobserved confounders may remain); limited external validity (single-country Pakistan sample with specific military–state dynamics); sample size and low prevalence of military directors may reduce statistical power for interaction tests; collinearity among governance covariates and moderator may inflate variance estimates; changing regulatory, political, or audit-market environments over 2010–2022 may confound time trends; aggregation of real EM components into indices can mask heterogeneous firm-level tactics; instrument proliferation and weak-instrument concerns in GMM can compromise inference; results do not identify precise causal mechanisms (discipline, networks, reputation) beyond statistical association.
